opus-5.5.text:
I think this is one of the most important open questions right now, and my view has shifted over time.

There's a long-standing argument, Yann LeCun has made it very forcefully, that you shouldn't learn a world model by generating pixels. The world is full of unpredictable detail: the exact texture of leaves, the ripples on water. If you force a model to reconstruct all of that, it spends enormous capacity on things that don't matter for understanding or decision-making. So the non-generative camp says: predict in an abstract representation space, learn what's predictable, and ignore the rest. JEPA-style methods and contrastive learning come from that philosophy.

I find that argument elegant, and I think it's partly right. But look at what has actually worked at scale. In language, the generative approach, just predicting the next token, turned out to be extraordinarily powerful. Its biggest advantage is that the objective is unambiguous. You have a clear loss, it scales smoothly, and you don't need clever tricks to avoid collapse. Non-generative methods often need careful design: negative samples, stop-gradients, momentum encoders, all kinds of regularization to keep the representation from degenerating. That engineering fragility matters a lot when you want to scale to trillions of tokens or huge amounts of video.

On the other hand, vision is not language. A text token is already a compressed, human-designed abstraction. A pixel is not. So next-pixel or next-frame prediction doesn't automatically give you the semantic structure that next-token prediction gives you in language. That's the real tension. In language, generation and understanding are almost the same thing. In vision, they can come apart. You can generate beautiful video without really understanding physics, and you can have good representations that can't generate anything.

So where do I land? I don't think it's a strict either-or. Practically, I think the most promising direction is generative modeling in a well-designed latent space. You first learn a compressed representation that throws away irrelevant detail, which is the non-generative insight, and then you do generative, autoregressive or diffusion-style prediction in that space, which gives you the scalable, unambiguous objective. Many of the strongest video models today already work roughly this way.

The deeper question is what a world model is for. If it's for producing content, generation is obviously the goal. If it's for an agent to plan and act, then what you really need is to predict consequences of actions at the right level of abstraction. Pixel fidelity is a means, not the end. I suspect the field will move toward judging world models by whether they improve reasoning and decision-making, not by how realistic their output looks. When that happens, the line between generative and non-generative will matter less than whether the model captures the causal structure of the world.

fable-5.1.text:
I think this question gets at something that's been on my mind a lot lately, and honestly my view has shifted over the past couple of years.

Let me start with the obvious framing. A generative world model tries to predict the future in the observation space itself — pixels, video frames, whatever the raw input is. A non-generative approach, something like JEPA that Yann LeCun has been advocating, says: don't predict the pixels, predict in some abstract representation space, and let the model decide what's worth predicting and what's just noise.

The argument for the non-generative side is pretty compelling on the surface. If I'm driving a car and there are leaves blowing in the wind, I don't need to predict the trajectory of every leaf. That's wasted capacity. A generative model is forced to spend bits on it, because reconstruction loss doesn't know the difference between a leaf and a pedestrian. So you abstract, you throw away the irrelevant stuff, you keep what matters for decisions.

But here's where I think the story is more complicated. The question of "what matters" is not known in advance. When you build the abstraction into the objective, you're making a bet about which information is useful, and the model has no way to recover information it was never asked to keep. Generative modeling is in some sense the most honest objective — you're saying, I don't know what's important, so I'll try to model everything, and let scale sort it out. That's basically the lesson of language modeling. Nobody designed next-token prediction to learn reasoning or world knowledge. It just fell out because the objective didn't throw anything away.

And the other thing is that non-generative methods have a persistent collapse problem. If you're predicting in a latent space that you also learn, the trivial solution is to make everything constant. So you need all these tricks — stop gradients, variance regularization, momentum encoders. Each one is a patch, and each one injects some prior that you didn't really justify. Generative models don't have that problem; the data itself is the anchor.

So where I've landed is something like this. I don't think the real dichotomy is generative versus non-generative. I think it's about what level of granularity you're predicting at, and whether the compression is learned or imposed. The thing that made language work is that text is already a compressed representation of the world — humans did the abstraction for us. For vision and physical interaction, we don't have that, and so the question of whether to learn the compression jointly with prediction, or to just brute-force the raw signal, is genuinely open.

My intuition right now is that generative approaches will go further than people expect, simply because they scale cleanly and the objective is unambiguous. But the compute cost of modeling high-dimensional observation spaces is real, and at some point you need the model to learn what to ignore. I suspect the eventual answer is a generative model that operates in a learned, but still decodable, latent space — so you keep the honesty of reconstruction as an anchor, but you don't pay for every pixel. The latent diffusion story is a hint in this direction. Whether that counts as generative or non-generative is kind of a semantic argument at that point.

The thing I'd caution against is picking a side based on elegance. The non-generative argument is more elegant. The generative argument has a better track record. In this field, track record usually wins.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: what do you need the world model to do? If you want to imagine possible futures, then a generative approach is a natural choice. Given the current situation and an action, you can generate what might happen next, including different possible outcomes.

But generating every detail of an observation can be unnecessary. For decision-making, you may care about where an object will move or whether an action will succeed, rather than the exact appearance of the scene. A non-generative approach can learn to predict those relevant properties in a representation space without reconstructing everything.

The challenge is deciding what information you can afford to leave out. A compact representation can be efficient, but it may discard something that becomes important for a new task. And a generative model can produce something that looks plausible without getting the consequences of an action right.

So I wouldn’t treat this as a choice with one universal winner. I’d ask whether the model captures the structure needed for prediction and control, and whether that structure transfers to new situations. You might ultimately want a combination: a representation that supports efficient reasoning, with generation where you actually need to explore alternative futures.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the choice depends on what you want the world model to do. If the goal is to generate possible futures—to imagine what an agent might see after taking an action—then a generative approach is very natural. But generating every detail of an observation can also be expensive, and many of those details may be irrelevant to making a decision.

A non-generative approach can instead learn to predict in a representation space: what aspects of the environment will change, what will remain stable, and what matters for the task. The challenge is making sure that representation preserves enough information for planning, especially when the agent encounters something new.

So I wouldn’t frame this as one approach being universally better. I would ask: What must the model predict, how should it represent uncertainty, and how will those predictions support action? You might use a compact predictive representation for most decisions and a generative component when you need to explore multiple possible outcomes. The key is whether the model captures the consequences of actions well enough to be useful.
